utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom This is case number IT-04-83-PT, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances, Prosecution first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom; for the Prosecution, the Prosecutor, Daryl Mundis and Aleksandar Kontic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. Nicholas Robson, we are the Defence counsel for General Rasim Delic, and with us here are our associates, Lejla Gluhic, Lana Deljkic, and Asja Zujo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. We are here this afternoon in an urgent hearing on a request for a referral of the case, the Delic case, as it was filed on the 5th of July of this year. The Chamber would very much like to hear further submissions of the parties and would like to focus on the following issue. The Delic case was not considered an appropriate case for referral until the present request. What now has changed in the character of the case, especially focusing on level of responsibility and gravity of the crimes so as to cause an urgent request for referral, and what further are the procedural consequences of a, if I could say it, five-minutes-to-12 referral procedure, both for the case as planned to start next Monday before this Tribunal and in view of the referral proceedings, and in view of proceedings, if the case would be referred as requested. The Chamber would like to give, initially, not more than 20 minutes to each party to make additional submissions. For the Defence, it's good to know that the Chamber -- that the Chamber, but when I am saying the Chamber, of course, you would also need further explanation of why there are only two judges. That is because Judge Parker is not available due to Tribunal business and that the two remaining Judges of this Referral Bench, as appointed this morning, have decided that it would be in the interest of justice to proceed. So further submissions are requested from the parties, but it's good for the Defence to know that the Chamber has read a public filing, this Referral Bench has read a public filing in the Delic case, in which a response is given to a request by the Prosecution to suspend all proceedings in the Delic case. As usual, before this Referral Bench, if it's clearly put on the record that the parties or the Chamber has seen a public filing or a public decision, then it is clear that we can take that into consideration as something now known and on the record known to the Bench. Mr. Mundis, could I give you an opportunity first to make additional submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution has some prepared comments that we would wish to put on to the record. I believe that these comments will encapsulate and address the specific questions which the Referral Bench would like addressed; and, of course, in the event that our comments are inadequate in that respect, we will certainly entertain any questions that the Referral Bench may have. Let me, Your Honours, start by acknowledging our appreciation that the Referral Bench was able to hear our urgent application in perhaps what might be considered record speed here at the Tribunal. We do express our regrets, however, that the representatives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina have been unable to attend due to the emergency nature of this hearing. It is our submission that prior to the Referral Bench rendering any decision, that they be offered the opportunity to make their views known on this matter. I will put on the record that we have had some informal oral discussions with the authorities, and they are prepared to take this case and their position is that they are able to take this case and afford all due process rights to the accused in the event the case were to be referred. Let me start by saying that while the Trial Chamber's oral decision under Rule 73 bis is the precipitating factor in this 11 bis application of the Prosecutor, the principles underlying the Prosecution motion must in our submission be considered on the merits, notwithstanding the late timing of this application, as the Presiding Judge indicated at 12 minutes to -- or five minutes to midnight. In other words, our view is that the fact that the case is scheduled to start in a few days should not impact upon the merits of our 11 bis application; and, of course, pursuant to the very terms of 11 bis, such applications must be made prior to the start or the commencement of the trial, which in our view we made as soon as it became clear to us, for the reasons which I'll be elaborating upon, it has become -- this case has become proper, if you will, for referral under 11 bis. Of the remaining cases to be tried before this International Tribunal, the Delic case is probably the only case that fits within the scope of Rule 11 bis. Let me also indicate, just by way of procedural background, that more than 15 months ago the Prosecution filed a motion seeking leave to amend the indictment in this case to include liability under Article 7(1) and to include crimes for which the accused was allegedly involved, involving Bugonja, Grabovica, and Uzdol. This motion was denied on the grounds that it could have impacted upon the start date of the trial, even though the case was not docketed. In our submission, the practical effect of that decision, approximately one year ago, was to significantly reduce the number of crimes for which the accused is to stand trial. The recent decision of the current Trial Chamber has had the real effect of further reducing the size of this case, since the Prosecution, under the time and witness limitations imposed upon us, will be able to present only a truncated picture of the accused's total alleged criminality. There are, Your Honours, important principles involved in this case, principles which go to the heart of the independence of the Office of the Prosecutor. Namely, there comes a point where the Prosecution is unable to prevent -- to present the full scope of the alleged criminality of an accused. While this may not present problems in larger cases, where representative counts or charges may nevertheless be presented, this is not the situation in smaller cases, such as in the Delic indictment, where the impact of Rule 73 bis has greater relative impacts. At the outset of the discussion concerning the impact of Rule 73 bis(C) decision, let me stress that the Trial Chamber's oral decision, which is the direct result of why we are here today, does not require the Prosecution to drop any counts or any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it the cause and not the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- does not require the Prosecution to drop any counts or any charges, but that is in effect, Your Honours, the practical impacts of the decision. As a result of the Trial Chamber's decision of 2 July, Monday of this week, the time available to the Prosecution has meant that choices must be made about how we are to proceed with the case. These choices have led to the unfortunate conclusion that the case, as it could be presented in the time made available to the Prosecution, is such that the case now clearly falls within the ambit of Rule 11 bis, and I will elaborate upon that in just a few moments. While the Prosecution understands the policies underlying Rule 73 business, and although the Prosecutor vehemently opposed the adoption of that Rule, the OTP has obligingly accepted it since it was lawfully adopted. Moreover, we understand that the purpose of today's hearing is not to re-litigate the 73 bis decision of the Trial Chamber, but it is our view, our position, that it is necessary to understand why that decision has led to the application under Rule 11 bis; and in order to do that, I need to briefly explain, in our view, what that decision means to the Prosecution. As Your Honours are aware, the Trial Chamber ordered, under 73 bis(C), the Prosecution to call 55 witnesses and that the Prosecution case would have a total of 170 hours, including direct examination, cross-examination, redirect examination, questions from the Bench, and procedural matters. For more than two years, the Prosecution has consistently indicated that our case would require four to five months and that approximately 75 witnesses would be required to prove the Prosecution case. At no point in the earlier proceedings, until one week before the trial was scheduled to start, was the Prosecution put on notice that its proposed length of time or the number of witnesses we had proposed was excessive. At no point in the earlier proceedings was the Prosecution invited to reduce the size of its case pursuant to Rule 73 bis. While the Prosecution will be filing additional urgent submissions before the Trial Chamber on this matter later today, in light of the fact that the Trial Chamber has refused to grant our request for a suspension of the proceedings, pending the outcome of this referral process, the Prosecution does not have a sense of optimism that this issue will be successfully resolved prior to the anticipated commencement of the trial. Thus, if this Referral Bench is of the view that the Rule 11 bis application is premature, in light of the possibility that the Trial Chamber may grant the Prosecution relief in the future, the Prosecution submits that events may, and I stress the word "may," unfold in such a way that there is no indictment to refer. Under the conditions imposed upon the Prosecution by the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution will be unable to lead evidence with respect to one of the alleged crime bases in the indictment; namely, the Maljine-Bikosi components of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Mundis. It is your case, then, isn't it, that in one way or another, the Trial Chamber's decision, 73 bis(C) decision is to be revoked, then the case will become appropriate to be heard at this Tribunal. Otherwise, it would be inappropriate to refer the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In short, and again, we will be making further urgent submissions later today, if the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is that urgent motion? That being the case, the proper step for you to take is to appeal the decision, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we made a determination that based upon, number 1, based upon the language of Rule 73 bis(F), which allows the Prosecution to request additional time or additional witnesses after the commencement of the trial, that the likelihood of an appeal on this issue would not be successful because Rule 73 bis explicitly allows for reconsideration of the decision concerning the number of witnesses and the amount of time available. Moreover, there was some concern about whether we would be in a position to have the trial suspended while that appeal was pending for the simple reason that with the 170 hour limitation what we are now talking about is a Prosecution case lasting nine and a half to ten weeks, by which point it's unlikely that any appeal would be resolved before the Prosecution case was over. But to return to your earlier question, yes, it is our position that the Rule 73 bis(C) oral decision has made it impossible for the Prosecution to proceed on even the indictment that we have now, which is a relatively, and I stress "relatively," small case. And it's, I believe, the smallest case among those cases yet to be tried before the International Tribunal, of course, excluding ongoing cases. But of the remaining case that is have yet to start, the case against Rasim Delic is by far the smallest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question to add to that, Mr. Mundis. You are certainly aware of the case law of this Referral Bench, that we always give decisions and consider applications on the basis of the operative indictment at that moment. What you are telling us at this moment is that the indictment, as it stands, cannot be heard -- at least the case cannot be presented by the Prosecution; therefore, you request referral. And you say that since the case will be reduced, that would make the case an appropriate case for referral. At the same time, we at this moment have a request in front of us on the basis of the operative indictment, so, therefore, you are speculating, or at least you are arguing your case, on the basis of an indictment which is not before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we understand that what we are talking about is referral of the indictment as it stands now. The point we are trying to make is that because of the decision of the Trial Chamber, it is impossible for the Prosecution to proceed on the basis of that indictment, the totality of that indictment. In effect, what the result of that decision means that we will be unable to proceed on that indictment. I'm by no means saying that the Trial Chamber would be referring an indictment that's not properly before it, or the Referral Bench. What I am saying is that notwithstanding the fact that we won't even be able to proceed against the totality of the indictment, the fact of the matter is that the indictment, as it stands now, the amended indictment from July 2006, that indictment is the smallest indictment of any case yet to be tried before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be clear. Isn't it true that in the application, it has been clearly stated which portion of the indictment should be dropped because the Prosecution sees no possibility to pursue that portion of the indictment, not being able to present evidence, and that that reduces the case in such a way that it is now where it was not earlier, where it now becomes of a size that is appropriate for referral? And at the same time, we have in front of us a request for referral of the indictment, not with one portion taken out but the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's concern and perhaps that's simply the pleading was in part inartfully drafted. I do understand Your Honour's concern. Obviously, we are asking for the entire indictment, the amended indictment, as it stands now, to be referred, and, perhaps, our arguments in that sense were not as clear as they should be. Let me stress, however, that what we are talking about here is a relatively small case. And the more important factor in terms of the level of responsibility of the accused is that what distinguishes this from other cases which have been referred is the fact that this is a case alleging 7(3) liability only, which, of course, in our view, means that the level of responsibility of the accused is fundamentally different from those cases which allege both 7(1) and 7(3) liability or 7(1) liability only. It should be stressed that the accused is not charged with ordering these crimes or instigating them or even aiding and abetting them. Though he is no less culpable for his failure to act under Article 7(3) than he would be for the commission of crimes under 7(1), he does under this form of liability necessarily play a much smaller role in the commission of the murders or other crimes as alleged in the amended indictment. Cognizant of the time, Your Honours, let me just move on to one or two final points. With respect to the situation, again, in the absence of the authorities from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation in the judicial system of that country at present, we generally rely upon the submissions in our written motion, but let me stress one other point, with regard to the capability of the courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the judicial system in that state to deal with high profile war crimes cases. It should be said that there are currently -- that they are currently trying Momcilo Mandic, the former RS Minister of Justice, and Gojko Klickovic, the former RS Prime Minister. So the judicial system in Bosnia-Herzegovina is capable of trying very senior level accused. I have three final points. It is our submission, Your Honours, that if Rule 11 bis cannot be invoked in this case, under these circumstances, given the size of this case and the nature of the charges and the form of liability alleged, then surely there is no other case currently before this International Tribunal that would be the proper focus for transfer under that rule. In terms of the size of the case, it is certainly in line with other cases that have been the subject of Rule 11 bis transfers and is actually smaller than some of the cases that have been transferred. The Prosecution respectfully submits that the trial in this case cannot commence until this Referral Bench has rendered its decision on the issue of referral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a matter to be addressed to the Trial Chamber, not to the Referral Bench. The Referral Bench cannot give orders to the Trial Chamber whether or not to suspend the start of a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. And the final point would be the one which we stressed at the beginning that the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be afforded an opportunity to be heard on this matter, prior to the Referral Bench rendering its decision. If there are no further questions, those are the submissions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you not going to address the issue of the procedural impact of potential referral, if any, in particular in terms of the right of the accused to expeditious trial, if referred?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. Again, in terms of the impact on the right to an expeditious trial, if the case were to be referred, that would properly be a question to be put to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in terms of when or how quickly he would be brought to trial there. Let me stress, though, in terms of the impact here, that the accused has been on or was on provisional release pending this trial. He's been back in custody since the 25th of June 2007, to the extent that that has any impact upon the Referral Bench's thinking. In terms of the procedural impact upon a case which is scheduled to start in three days' time, again, we would submit that that is not something which is a proper consideration for the Referral Bench, but rather the case should be decided, the transfer of the case should be decided, on the merits of the application, not on its practical impacts upon the docket of the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, therefore, consider that the discretion of the Referral Bench should just ignore all procedural impacts of its decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, to the extent, Your Honours, that the -- what the Referral Bench is concerned about would be a hole in the docket or the inability of the Tribunal to put on a seventh case during 2007, then, yes, we would say that that's not something that the Referral Bench should take into consideration. If there are other procedural impacts, perhaps I've misunderstood the question, but our submission would be that, no, it would not be a proper exercise of the Referral Bench's discretion to consider the fact that the case is scheduled to start very shortly; and in the absence of this case starting, there would be a hole in the docket for a few months perhaps. That, in our submission, is not something that the Referral Bench should take into consideration, but rather the merits of the case in terms of the indictment and the level of responsibility of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Ms. Vidovic, 20 minutes for you as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think I'll be relatively brief. Your Honours, first of all, I would like to tackle an additional argument of the Prosecutor today. Mr. Mundis said that, unofficially, they contacted the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know which authorities he meant, and that the position there was that the General Delic trial, they stated their position on the fact of the trial being referred. I would be very surprised, Your Honours, if the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina presented the view that they accept the case, because this would be quite contrary to the position taken by those same authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it came to the case against Dragomir Milosevic, where they quite clearly stated that they consider that the accused, who are at a high level of responsibility, should be tried here in The Hague. However, I do think that the position taken by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina is not of decisive importance in these criminal proceedings. Your Honours, although I had certain dilemma before this meeting as to what the true and actual reason was for the fact that General Delic was asked to be referred to Sarajevo, I really don't have them any more. I have gained the opinion that the Prosecution is angry because the Trial Chamber has asked them to present 55 witnesses during a period of three months. Now, the Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Kwon, luckily is with us here today as well, and he will remember that the Prosecution from the very beginning envisaged about three months. They deemed that to be enough time for their case, and I issued a warning and said that that was not a realistic estimate. However, whatever the case may be, and we expound that in our response and don't want to dwell on that, the Prosecution did have the necessary procedural possibilities, if it was dissatisfied, to ask leave to file an appeal; that is to say, it had the possibility that after the beginning of trial, it asked for change in the ruling of the Trial Chamber so as to allow them additional witnesses and additional time. Now, why is it that the Prosecution, at this point in time, is taking this kind of step? It is up to you, Your Honours, to decide and rule. However, I should like to focus my attention on the reasons pursuant to Rule 11 bis, which the Prosecution sets out in its motion, as being standards which correspond to the demands of Rule 11 bis of the rules of procedure and evidence, for the case to be referred to Bosnia and Herzegovina. First of all, I would like to stress, Your Honours, or rather, I'd like to explain what the Prosecutor quite obviously doesn't feel to be important; whereas, I consider it to be a substantive matter in all criminal trials in the world. The accused is here since February 2005, waiting to go to trial, and he has spent three months in detention. Pursuant to Article 20 of the Statute, he has the right to a fair and expeditious trial, as the Statute states. According to Article 21(4)(C) of the Statute, he enjoys the right to be tried without undue postponement, and the Prosecutor, in his motion, states that it is in the interests of justice that the case be referred pursuant to Rule 11 bis to the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Quite the reverse is true, Your Honours. The interests of justice demand that the trial of General Rasim Delic start on Monday, the 9th of July 2007, when it was scheduled to do so, and that there should be no postponement. It is quite -- it is not at all serious in this stage to bring matters of this kind. It is unfair to the accused. It is unfair to us here in the Defence team. The accused is psychologically ready to go to trial. We are ready and prepared to go to trial. We have invested material resources to ensure that we have the necessary premises and facilities to go ahead, and witnesses are lined up to begin testimony in two or three days time. Now, if the Trial Chamber were to rule in favour of the Prosecution, we would of course appeal, and the accused would have to wait until the appeals procedure meets its conclusion, then he would have to go into a series of other procedures while being referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The indictment would have to be amended in conformity with the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, ultimately, an assessment of evidence would have to be aligned with those other requests. So the Prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have to study an enormous amount of material, over 3.000 exhibits and pieces of evidence in this trial. The Prosecutor, furthermore, says that so far six cases have been referred to the courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, I have done my best to check this out and to see how far those cases and those individuals had to wait to go to trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the result is at least ten months. Ten months is the minimum, and the average is between ten and 13 months. So it is quite certain, Your Honours, that General Delic, too, would have to wait for many months for his case to go to trial, and that certainly is not in the interests of justice, Your Honours. And it would have a vital effect on his health and on his family as well. He is an individual who gave himself up to the Court. He asked that his trial -- he go to trial straight away. He did not wish to avoid responsibility, quite the contrary. He wished this Tribunal to establish the facts as soon as possible. Next, Your Honour, the Prosecutor has claimed here that the accused would have a fair trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, Your Honour, I have gained the impression that the Prosecutor isn't very concerned about this matter, whether the accused would be given a fair trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina or not. It is true that the Criminal Codes of Bosnia-Herzegovina do not have the death penalty and that six cases have been referred there. However, Your Honours, I would like to request that you bear in mind the fact that none of those six cases are cases of such a high-ranking individual as this one, and it is difficult to see that the accused with such a high level of command responsibility, particularly in the political relationships which prevail in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, would indeed be given a fair trial. If that court through its practice has never had occasion to try a case of that nature. The Prosecutor today mentioned two cases: Mandic and Klickovic. Your Honours, I doubt that you know very much about those cases, but I know a great deal about those cases, and what I do know is this: Those cases have nothing to do on a factual level or legal level, particularly not on a legal level, and serious legal issues are raised, as would be those issues that we have here in the case before you. So, Your Honours, please bear in mind the fact that the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina is overloaded. It has thousands of cases pending trial, and they are seeking ways and means over the past year or two to get through this enormous amount faster. They have organisational problems. And let me just mention that just one of the six cases has been led to completion, and the person who was convicted in that particular case has escaped from prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, may I stop you there? I think at the beginning of this hearing, I told you what the Chamber would like to focus on this afternoon, and that is not the full range of follow-up of cases referred to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Mundis had said something about it. You gave a few observations on it, but further details do not assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will speak of the weight first of all. The Prosecution refers to a relatively small number of victims, the limited time span, and limited territory and locality encompassed in the indictment when it comes to this case and the gravity of it. At the moment, we have 100 victims in the indictment, of which 79 are killings. The rest are victims of torture and rape, as alleged in the indictment. Now, even if the Prosecution were to give up on the part of the indictment which refers to the events in Maljine - and there are obviously manipulations with that because no decision exists in that respect - we would still have 74 victims, of which 55 were killings. And it would be difficult to say that they are not serious, that these killings are not serious, even when compared to other cases tried before this Tribunal. They are indeed very serious accusations and counts. Now, the Prosecution is trying to explain the fact that the case is not a difficult one, in that it was limited in time to three short periods, spanning two years. Your Honours, that is no argument. It is not an argument which can hold water, because in a very short period of time, very serious crimes can, of course, be committed, and we have examples of cases of that kind being tried at the Tribunal already. Then, he said that the indictment is limited geographically, so both in terms of time and geography, none of which or neither of which are factors on the basis of which one could weigh up the gravity and seriousness of the case, particularly not when it comes to somebody who held a high ranking command responsibility of the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is what the accused was. Your Honours, our client stands accused of exerting effective control over all the fighters, the Mujahedin, and all the other units involved in the various events. So in actual terms, the indictment and the pre-trial motions and the evidence produced by the Prosecution under the 65 ter list show that the Prosecutor is studying the entire period from the arrival of the Mujahedin in Bosnia, the alleged joint facts, in order to control -- to confirm the BH army control over all these fighters and effective control of General Delic over them. The question of control over the Mujahedin is in itself a highly complex question and cannot be viewed without investigating and looking into their overall effects and actions; and for that reason, this case is a highly complex case and will certainly have leverage in a series of legal arguments, et cetera. Now, as far as responsibility, General Delic, in military hierarchy and political hierarchy, in the indictment period, occupied the top most level of responsibility that is possible in state. He stands accused that as the commander of the Main Staff of the BH army, and it is alleged that he was a member of the Presidency as well, that he acted in the way in which the indictment stands out. Rule 11 bis demands that the Trial Chamber, in seeing whether the conditions are met, have in view the Security Council resolution 1534 to consider the gravity of crimes, and to accuse those positioned in the top level of hierarchies. And in view of the crimes committed, it is quite certain that the Prosecutor had in mind both these factors when raising the indictment, and they raised the indictment after the Security Council resolution was passed in 2004. Now suddenly, just prior to the trial, he suddenly does not consider that the case is serious enough to be tried by this Court. The resolution, I mentioned, demands that the Tribunal focus on cases of top level responsibility and to refer to national courts medium level and low level responsibility cases. Your Honours, it was a pleasure for me to read that, although General Delic did indeed hold a high rank, that his real role in the crimes was minimal. That's what the Prosecutor wrote, and I was happy to read that. However, let's see what the indictment says about the position of General Delic and look at the counts and charges against him. Paragraph 3, for example, says that General Delic was appointed commander of the Main Staff of the BH army by the Presidency and that he remained in that position for two and a half years. So the period in the indictment is two and a half years occupying that post. As the commander of the Main Staff, he was the top most ranking officer subordinate only to the Presidency. He had general responsibilities and responsible for the functioning of the army, the planning of military affairs and in command of actions and operations, which resulted in alleged crimes being committed; and that he ordered the formation of the El Mujahid unit and the disbanding of the El Mujahid units. Your Honour, quite simply, what the Prosecution sets out in his motion, and what he has written down in his indictment, is not consistent. And the Defence considers that, in the case of the accused General Delic, these are all serious accusations, serious allegations, and invoke top level responsibility, precisely the kind of responsibility for which this Tribunal was set up in the first place, by the United Nations, expounding their stands through the resolution I mentioned a moments ago, and stated that only medium and lower level cases be referred to local courts. This reassertion was confirmed by the case law here in the Tribunal, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Rasevic and Savo Todovic, for example, when the Trial Chamber ruled wearing in mind the fact that the International Tribunal should focus on trying top level individuals, having committed top level crimes, and to transfer all other cases; that is to say, of individuals who do not hold that top level responsibility, that they should be referred to national jurisdictions. And I'd like to invoke the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic, when the Trial Chamber said that he was a commander for over a period of one year, and that there was just one level of responsibility above him. And the Trial Chamber went even further and ruled that the commander was of a lower rank than is our own client, and that even that level of responsibility demanded that this Tribunal try the case. So, for all these reasons, Your Honour, I move that the Prosecution's motion be rejected to have the case transferred pursuant to Rule 11 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. Before I give an opportunity for a final round, I would have a few questions. Mr. Mundis, Ms. Vidovic has referred to the decision in the Dragomir Milosevic case, in which the level of responsibility next to the role of an accused in the commission of the crimes has been dealt with; and if I would draw your attention to the decision, the Lukic Referral Decision, which is not a final decision yet, but in which it says that the level of responsibility of an accused relates both to the role of the accused in the commission of the alleged offences and to the position and rank of the accused in the hierarchy; whereas, you have spent quite some words on the role of the accused, however, not many words yet on the rank of the accused in the hierarchy. So I would first like to hear your response to what Ms. Vidovic said in relation to Milosevic and what the Referral Bench has decided in the Lukic referral case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is beyond dispute that throughout the indictment period, the accused Rasim Delic was the most senior military commander in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, there is no dispute about that. So, in effect, he was the most senior military commander of the Armija during the period covered by the indictment. We focus our attention, Your Honours, on the level of responsibility, in the sense of this being an Article 7(3) only case, and there is a quantitative and qualitative difference between a military commander who is ordering crimes and a military commander who is failing to prevent or failing to punish crimes; and in that respect, that's what distinguishes this case from the Dragomir Milosevic case, in terms of the issue of responsibility of the accused. But for the record, there is no doubt that this accused was the most senior military commander in the army, and the Prosecution is not trying to hide behind the fact that he, or is in any way suggesting, that he wasn't the most senior military commander. But, again, when we are looking at a relatively small number of crimes for which the accused is alleged to have failed to prevent or failed to punish the perpetrators of those crimes, that's a very different situation than someone such as Dragomir Milosevic and his role in the alleged crimes in the city of Sarajevo during the indictment period in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not that familiar with the history of the Delic case. There was an indictment chronology. I had no possibility to revisit all the earlier versions of the indictment, but do I understand well, from annex A, that the scope of the indictment, as it is now, is actually the same as it was in the very beginning, that is, in December 2004? That's two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So a lot has happened but not much has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you are asking the referral on the basis of the operative indictment at this moment. In 2004, especially in December 2004, I think the referral discussion was already very vivid at that time. Nevertheless, the Prosecution, at that time, indicting Mr. Delic has chosen to bring him before the Tribunal on this indictment, rather than under the rules-of-the-road ask for Prosecution in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you have any comments on that? I mean, it's not an old indictment of 1997, but it's a relatively recent indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just have a moments to consult with the Prosecutor on that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time the accused Rasim Delic was indicted, he fell within those cases which were among the last to be indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal. The Prosecution, in submitting the indictment in December 2004, because of the completion strategy deadlines with respect to investigations and the indictment process, had always been of the position that we would seek leave to amend that indictment once remaining crime bases were consolidated and the investigative material that we had compiled was examined. So I will be very transparent with this Referral Bench that it had always been our intention to seek leave to amend, which we did. Those applications, as I've indicated, and as Judge Kwon is well aware, those applications were unsuccessful. We had always believed that, given the fact that the accused was not likely to be tried for a couple of years, that the impact of those -- of that motion seeking leave to amend the indictment would be granted, for the simple reason that it would have no impact upon the rites of the accused, because sufficient time would be available for the Defence to adequately investigate and prepare for trial based on those amendments. That motion was unsuccessful, and that explains why the indictment, notwithstanding the steps taken subsequently, remains virtually the same as it was in December 2004, or as initially confirmed by Judge Agius in early 2005. That's about all I can say about that. But having confirmed with the Prosecutor, it had always been our intention to amend the indictment, and we tried to do that without success.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you told us that you do not want to re-litigate the 73 bis decision of the Trial Chamber. At the same time, implicitly, you do, because I think the Trial Chamber in its oral decision has identified that on the list of witnesses, too many witnesses. I do understand that to be an accumulation of witnesses beyond what is needed, so, therefore, there are too many witnesses. Now you say we can't do it with any less witnesses, which actually comes down to a criticism of the finding of the Trial Chamber in that respect. You're asking us to follow that criticism rather than to accept the finding of the Trial Chamber, which says you can prove your case in less time and with less witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be very brief on this point, as I've indicated earlier, we will be filing an urgent motion later this afternoon to re-seize the Trial Chamber on that point. And what I want to say in this respect is that due to the timing of the Trial Chamber's decision on Monday and the anticipated start date of this trial, and the requirement that a referral motion come prior to the commencement of trial, we felt, the Office of the Prosecutor felt, that we, under these circumstances, had no choice but to seize the President of a request for referral to the Referral Bench. We will be revisiting that issue as I've indicated, but again the Prosecution is not optimistic in that respect. I also want to add one other point in response to something Mrs. Vidovic said, which I think is extremely probative and relevant on this point. A few moments ago, in explaining why this case should stay here, Mrs. Vidovic indicated the complexity of the factual matters with respect to the Mujahedin. It is precisely due to that complexity that the Prosecution submits, and will submit to the Trial Chamber, that 55 witnesses and 170 hours is not adequate for us to prove our case. Cases involving 7(3) liability only are extremely problematic and difficult to prove before this institution. They are very similar, in many respects, to purely circumstantial cases, whereby large numbers of witnesses and large numbers of documents are required to prove the necessary elements with respect to effective control and notice, particularly when it comes to issues involving failure to punish and proving the negative of that failure. In that respect, we would submit that, again, we will be seizing the Trial Chamber. I understand the position that the Referral Bench feels that it's in with respect to the Trial Chamber; but due to the timing issues, we did not feel that we could wait until the morning, before the commencement of the trial, to file the motion that's currently before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis, I'm not blaming you for once having decided that referral would be appropriate, that you then immediately filed it, because otherwise you would have been late under Rule 11 bis. Of course. The issue is whether referral is appropriate; then the timing is, I would say, an inevitable consequence. You had to do it immediately, there is no doubt about that. Then, Ms. Vidovic, you listed quite a number of matters as relevant. You said, "We have studied all the material. We have prepared." Of course, I do see the psychological consequences. But that work would still serve the Defence of Mr. Delic, if the case would be referred, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't receive any translation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English channel now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear it. Could you please restart, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, no, because the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina has its own procedure, especially its own view of evidence and how evidence is treated. It's quite different from here, absolutely, Your Honours. Your Honours, rest assured, the accused would wait for a long time for his trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any challenge, Mr. Mundis, in the ten month as a minimal period assessment by Ms. Vidovic; that is, the time from referral to the start of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution doesn't have at hand the minimal amount of time available, but my colleague, Mr. Kontic, assured me that's approximately, as we would say in the ballpark, in terms of the amount of time. Before the Referral Bench rises, if I could just address one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to give, for final submissions, five minutes to each. If you would say, "I've no further questions, I'd now make my final submissions," then the clock starts running now. Mr. Mundis, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't intend to actually take the full five minutes because I believe the issue has been adequately briefed and orally addressed this afternoon, but I do want to, again, stress the Prosecution position. And I fully understand and appreciate that the Referral Bench has no ability to impact the potential start date of the trial, but what we are concerned about is simply that this process is being rushed. We need to keep, our position is, we need to keep open the door to ensure that justice is done in this case, whether it's done here or whether it's done in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our position is that this case is now more appropriately -- would be more appropriately heard before the court -- the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But what we want to ensure is that this trial does not commence before the Referral Bench has had the full opportunity to consider the arguments of the parties and of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, again, we will be seizing the Trial Chamber of motions or of a motion concerning a number of issues that we've discussed here today. We have nothing further to add and, again, we want to thank the Referral Bench for making it possible to have this emergency urgent hearing this afternoon on such short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, final submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mrs. Vidovic has asked me to make come closing submissions, which I'll make briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my submissions concern the level of responsibility of the accused, which you've obviously got to take into account. My first point is in looking at the seniority of General Delic, I would reiterate that within Rule 11 bis, the Trial Chamber is required to take consideration of the Security Council resolution 1534. Point 5 of that resolution clearly states that the Tribunal should concentrate on the most senior leaders. Point 6 of that resolution requires the Tribunal to consider measures that look at the transfer of cases involving intermediate and lower level rank accused to competent national jurisdictions. In this case, it's clear that General Delic, as the commander of the Main Staff of the Bosnian army, was the most senior military commander in Bosnia. He was responsible for around 250.000 men. He was a permanent position in which he served until the year 2000. And, again, I would just draw your attention to the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber in the Rasevic and Todovic decision, that's the decision of the 4th of September 2006. And, again, the Appeals Chamber emphasised the importance of Trial Chambers concentrating on the Prosecution and trial of the most serious leaders suspected of being responsible for crimes. Moving from that point, Your Honour, I would turn to the issue of General Delic's actual role in the commission of the alleged crimes. The Prosecution has placed a lot of importance on that and what it would seem, Your Honour, is that they are taking a rather contradictory position with regard to that point. On the one hand, the Prosecution seem to be saying that the Delic case is a relatively small case, that because he is only charged with responsibility under Article 7(3) and because the Trial Chambers in the past have routinely handed down low sentences for Article 7(3) command responsibility cases, this is an indication that this is a less grave case and, therefore, you can send it or refer it back to Bosnia. We've just heard a moment ago from Mr. Mundis, and he has explained to us about the problems involved in Article 7(3) cases. And, again, he's emphasised the particular dilemmas involved in this case. We've heard that the case will involve the allegation that General Delic had exercised effective control over the Mujahedin. Mr. Mundis said this was an extremely problematic matter. Your Honours, my submission would be, then, this is an excellent reason to keep the matter here before this Tribunal, rather than referring it back to Bosnia. So, Your Honours, those are my final submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider how to proceed. It has not decided how to proceed. So, therefore, it could be that the Chamber would come back to the parties and ask for further oral or written submissions, but it's also possible that the Chamber will not do that. Therefore, we stand adjourned sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.33 p.m.
